faster than the monitoring cadence could detect it, the trade is unavailable regardless of program quality.
Irreversibility  forecloses  the  trade. Where  the  harm  from  an  incorrect  output  cannot  be  undone,
postmarket detection is not a mitigation — it is an audit of damage already done.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that flexibility to accept greater premarket uncertainty in exchange for postmarket monitoring could be applied to the highest-risk devices unless an explicit boundary is stated.
positions.requested_fda_action: State affirmatively that reduced premarket evidence is not available for devices falling in the high-consequence, high-activity region of the two-axis risk grid, so the flexibility is bounded on its face.
positions.public_summary: Accepts the concept of trading premarket uncertainty for postmarket monitoring but asks FDA to state explicitly that this flexibility is unavailable for devices in the high-consequence, high-activity region of the risk grid, bounding the approach on its face.
positions.source_passage:
I recommend CDRH state affirmatively that reduced premarket evidence is not available for devices in the
high-consequence, high-activity region of the risk grid, so that the flexibility is bounded on its face.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Calendar-based reassessment is mismatched to GenAI devices whose performance shifts discontinuously at the moment of a change rather than gradually over time, so fixed-interval review could miss safety-relevant degradation.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt an event-driven reassessment cadence with a calendar floor (annual, or more frequent for higher-risk devices), with triggers including model version/weight changes (manufacturer- or provider-initiated), prompt/instruction/output template changes, retrieval corpus changes, input-distribution shifts beyond prespecified bounds, sampling configuration changes, and complaint or adjudicated-error thresholds.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The commenter explicitly includes changes to the underlying model version or weights initiated by the model provider, not just the manufacturer, as a mandatory reassessment trigger.

positions.public_summary: Finds FDA's three postmarket evaluation approaches sensible and complementary, but recommends replacing calendar-driven cadence with event-driven triggers plus a calendar floor. Proposed triggers include model version/weight changes by manufacturer or model provider, prompt, retrieval corpus, sampling, input-distribution, and complaint/error thresholds.
positions.source_passage:
The three approaches described are sensible and complementary. My substantive recommendation concerns
cadence: it should be event-driven with a calendar floor, not calendar-driven.
Calendar-based reassessment is poorly matched to a technology whose performance changes discontinuously
at the moment of a change rather than continuously with time. I recommend triggering events include, at
minimum: any change to the underlying model version or weights, whether initiated by the manufacturer or
the model provider; any change to system prompts, instructions, or output templates; any change to a retrieval
corpus or knowledge source; any measured shift in the input distribution beyond prespecified bounds; any
change in the deployed sampling configuration; and any accumulation of complaints or adjudicated errors
exceeding a prespecified threshold. A calendar floor — annual, or more frequent for higher-risk devices —
should catch slow drift that trips no discrete trigger.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that postmarket performance monitoring and reassessment triggers would be maintained as a process separate from existing design-change controls, and states that parallel processes diverge.
positions.requested_fda_action: Define postmarket monitoring triggers (e.g., reassessment/re-benchmarking events) as change-control triggers within the manufacturer's quality management system, so monitoring obligations are integrated with existing design-change procedures rather than run as a standalone process.
positions.public_summary: Accepts postmarket reassessment triggers but asks FDA to define them as change-control triggers inside the manufacturer's quality management system, integrated with existing design-change procedures rather than maintained as a separate monitoring process, warning that parallel processes diverge.
positions.source_passage:
From  a  quality-system  perspective  these  should  be  defined  as  change-control  triggers  within  the
manufacturer's QMS, so that the postmarket monitoring obligation is integrated with existing design-change
procedures rather than maintained as a separate process. Parallel processes diverge.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Human review of every output is not feasible for high-throughput GenAI devices, so machine-based supervisory agents are effectively unavoidable at scale; the central concern is their trustworthiness rather than whether they should be allowed.
positions.requested_fda_action: Accept automated supervision as a practical necessity and focus regulatory attention on how to make machine-based supervisory agents trustworthy, rather than on whether to permit their use.

gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: The comment rests on the point that output volumes in high-throughput deployment make per-output human review infeasible, forcing reliance on automated assurance mechanisms.
gap_explanations.delegated_authority: It treats the delegation of oversight from humans to machine supervisory agents as effectively unavoidable, shifting the question to how such delegated supervision can be made trustworthy.

positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts machine-based supervisory agents for postmarket monitoring, arguing per-output human review is infeasible at high throughput. Frames the regulatory question as how to make automated supervision trustworthy rather than whether to permit it, without specifying reliability criteria.
positions.source_passage:
Automated supervision is probably unavoidable at the volumes involved — human review of every output is
not feasible for a high-throughput device — so the question is how to make it trustworthy rather than whether
to permit it.

positions.stakeholder_concern: A machine supervisory agent built on the same foundation model as the device it monitors shares that model's blind spots, producing correlated failures where the supervisor approves erroneous outputs and its agreement is mistaken for independent confirmation.
positions.requested_fda_action: Condition evidentiary use of supervisory agents on architectural independence — a model of a different family and provider than the supervised device — and, where full independence is impractical, require sponsors to characterize and report supervisor-device failure-mode correlation on a held-out error set, scaling monitoring credit to demonstrated independence.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment concerns oversight duties delegated to an automated supervisory agent and the conditions under which that agent's judgments may count as credible monitoring evidence.
gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: It ties assurance to the provenance of the underlying model, requiring a different model family and provider to avoid shared, supplier-inherited blind spots.

positions.public_summary: Accepts machine supervisory agents for postmarket monitoring but warns of correlated failure when supervisor and device share a foundation model. Asks FDA to require a different model family and provider, or reported failure-mode correlation on held-out errors, with monitoring credit scaled to demonstrated independence.
positions.source_passage:
The dominant risk is correlated failure.  A supervisory agent built on the same foundation model as the
device it monitors shares that model's blind spots. It will approve exactly the outputs that are wrong for
reasons the model family does not represent, and its agreement will be misread as independent confirmation.

Architectural  independence  as  a  condition  of  evidentiary  use. A  supervisory  agent  offered  as
postmarket evidence should be built on a model of a different family and provider than the supervised
device. Where full independence is impractical, the sponsor should characterize and report the correlation
in failure modes between supervisor and device on a held-out error set, and the monitoring program's
credit should scale with the demonstrated independence.

positions.stakeholder_concern: A machine-based supervisory agent functions as a measuring instrument whose own reliability is uncertain and can degrade; aggregate agreement statistics can look strong while sensitivity for detecting serious errors is near zero because most outputs are correct.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require that supervisory agents be validated like measuring instruments, reporting sensitivity for the specific harms of interest against sampled human adjudication rather than aggregate agreement, and re-measuring that sensitivity over time to account for supervisor drift.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment addresses oversight responsibility being handed to an automated supervisory agent and insists that agent's own error-detection capability be independently demonstrated and periodically re-verified.
gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: It ties continued postmarket assurance to ongoing sampled human adjudication and repeated re-measurement, raising how monitoring reliability is sustained over time rather than established once.

positions.public_summary: Accepts machine-based supervisory agents for postmarket monitoring only if the supervisor is validated as a measuring instrument: reporting sensitivity for specific harms against sampled human adjudication, not aggregate agreement, and re-measuring sensitivity over time as supervisor performance drifts.
positions.source_passage:
The supervisor is itself a measuring instrument and must be validated as one.  Report its sensitivity
for  the  specific  harms  of  interest  against  human  adjudication  on  a  sampled  basis  —  not  aggregate
agreement, which is dominated by the easy majority of correct outputs and can be high while sensitivity
for serious errors is near zero. Sensitivity must be re-measured over time, since the supervisor's own
performance drifts.

positions.stakeholder_concern: If a machine supervisory agent renders the final judgment in postmarket monitoring, there is no independent check remaining in the loop. The commenter sees value in machine-assisted triage but not in machine-made conclusions.
positions.requested_fda_action: Limit machine-based supervisory agents to prioritizing and sampling outputs for human review, and require that the adjudicated monitoring endpoint remain a human determination.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment addresses how much oversight authority may be delegated to an automated supervisory agent, insisting terminal adjudication stay with humans to preserve an independent check.

positions.public_summary: Accepts machine-based supervisory agents for postmarket monitoring only as triage tools that prioritize outputs and expand sampling for human review. Argues the final adjudicated judgment must remain human, since a monitoring program with a machine-made terminal decision lacks any independent check.
positions.source_passage:
The supervisor triages; it does not conclude.  Its appropriate role is prioritizing outputs for human
review and enabling broader sampling than humans could achieve unaided. The adjudicated endpoint
should  remain  human.  A  monitoring  program  whose  terminal  judgment  is  machine-made  has  no
independent check anywhere in the loop.

positions.stakeholder_concern: If a machine-based supervisory agent is treated as outside the device, changes to it could silently alter the device's monitoring properties without any reassessment.
positions.requested_fda_action: Treat the supervisory agent as part of the device system for change-control purposes, so that modifications to the supervisor trigger reassessment on the same terms as modifications to the device itself.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment addresses a machine agent to which oversight functions are delegated, arguing its own modifications must be governed because they change the assurance the monitoring provides.

positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts use of machine-based supervisory agents but asks FDA to treat the supervisor as part of the device system for change control, so that changes to the supervisory agent trigger the same reassessment as changes to the device.
positions.source_passage:
The supervisor is part of the device system  for change-control purposes. A change to the supervisory
agent changes the device's monitoring properties and should trigger reassessment on the same terms as a
change to the device.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that framing postmarket monitoring as a shared ecosystem could be read as shared responsibility, diluting the manufacturer's complaint-handling, investigation, and reporting obligations even when signals originate from clinicians, institutions, or societies.
positions.requested_fda_action: State explicitly in the paper that information may come from any source but the duty to investigate and act remains solely with the manufacturer, and that arrangements to receive third-party signal do not delegate any complaint-handling, investigation, or reporting obligations.

gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The comment directly addresses the risk that multi-actor postmarket signal collection blurs where regulatory duty sits, and asks FDA to fix accountability with the manufacturer.

positions.public_summary: Accepts that clinicians, health systems, and societies can supply postmarket signals, including outcome data manufacturers lack, but asks CDRH to state explicitly that manufacturers retain all complaint-handling, investigation, and reporting duties, so shared-ecosystem language is not read as shared responsibility.
positions.source_passage:
The accountability principle can be stated simply, and I recommend CDRH state it: information may come
from anywhere; the duty to investigate and act remains with the manufacturer.  Clinicians, institutions,
and societies can be valuable sources of signal, and health systems in particular hold the outcome data
manufacturers lack. But a manufacturer that has arranged to receive signal from third parties has not thereby
delegated any portion of its complaint-handling, investigation, or reporting obligations, and the paper should
say so directly to prevent the shared-ecosystem framing from being read as shared responsibility.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues postmarket monitoring for GenAI-enabled devices should build on existing complaint-handling and MDR structures, but warns that it is currently undefined what counts as a reportable event or malfunction for a generative output — for example, a clinically incorrect recommendation that the clinician recognizes and disregards, which under a conventional malfunction reading could make hallucinations reportable.
positions.requested_fda_action: Use the existing complaint-handling and MDR architecture rather than a parallel postmarket structure, and first clarify what constitutes a reportable event or device malfunction for generative outputs, including outputs caught and disregarded by a clinician.

gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: The commenter raises whether an incorrect generative output intercepted by a clinician constitutes a reportable malfunction, an issue about evaluating the device within the clinician-device system rather than the device alone.

positions.public_summary: Supports using existing complaint-handling and MDR structures rather than a parallel postmarket system, but says FDA must first define what counts as a reportable event or malfunction for generative outputs — including incorrect recommendations a clinician recognizes and disregards.
positions.source_passage:
I recommend building on the existing complaint-handling and MDR architecture rather than creating a
parallel  structure.  That  said,  I  want  to  flag  a  gap  that  I  believe  requires  attention  before  postmarket
monitoring can function at all for these devices:
It is currently unclear what constitutes a reportable event for a generative output. If a device produces a
clinically incorrect recommendation and the clinician recognizes and disregards it, has a device malfunction
occurred? Under a conventional reading, the device did not perform as intended, and a malfunction that could
cause or contribute to serious injury if it recurred is reportable — which would imply that hallucinations

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that postmarket monitoring roles for GenAI-enabled devices could be structured as a new, parallel reporting system separate from established device surveillance mechanisms.
positions.requested_fda_action: Build any postmarket monitoring roles and reporting expectations on the existing complaint-handling and medical device reporting (MDR) architecture rather than establishing a separate parallel structure.
positions.public_summary: The commenter accepts postmarket monitoring for GenAI-enabled devices but recommends that FDA structure it within existing complaint-handling and MDR frameworks rather than creating a separate, parallel reporting system.
positions.source_passage:
I recommend building on the existing complaint-handling and MDR architecture rather than creating a
parallel  structure.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states it is unclear whether a clinically incorrect generative output that a clinician recognizes and disregards constitutes a reportable device malfunction, and argues this unresolved ambiguity underlies every element of the postmarket section.
positions.requested_fda_action: Asks CDRH to define directly what constitutes a reportable event for generative outputs, and suggests a distinct aggregate reporting channel in which caught errors are reported as rates rather than individual MDRs to preserve signal without unmanageable event volume.

gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: The comment turns on whether an incorrect output intercepted by a clinician counts as a device malfunction, making reportability depend on the combined human-AI system rather than the model alone.

positions.public_summary: Commenter says FDA has not defined what counts as a reportable event when a generative output is clinically incorrect but caught by a clinician, and asks CDRH to resolve this, suggesting caught errors be reported as aggregate rates rather than individual MDRs.
positions.source_passage:
It is currently unclear what constitutes a reportable event for a generative output. If a device produces a
clinically incorrect recommendation and the clinician recognizes and disregards it, has a device malfunction
occurred? ... This ambiguity is consequential and unresolved, and every element of Section VI depends on how it is
settled. I recommend CDRH address it directly, and would suggest that the workable answer likely involves a
distinct, aggregate reporting channel for caught errors — reported as rates rather than as individual MDRs —
so that the signal is preserved without generating unmanageable individual-event volume.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Categorizing post-deployment modifications by the magnitude of the change may misallocate scrutiny; what matters is whether the locked premarket evaluation instrument (e.g., the benchmark suite) remains valid for the modified device.
positions.requested_fda_action: Retain the premarket competency assessment as a locked baseline, but scale re-benchmarking and evidence requirements according to whether a change invalidates the locked evaluation instrument rather than by the size of the change.
positions.public_summary: Supports using the premarket competency assessment as a locked baseline, but proposes that change categorization turn on whether the locked evaluation instrument remains valid for the modified device rather than on the magnitude of the change, since small changes may invalidate benchmarks.
positions.source_passage:
I support using the premarket competency assessment as a locked baseline. The organizing principle I would
propose for categorizing changes is this:  the question is not how large the change is, but whether the
locked evaluation instrument remains valid for the changed device.  A small change that invalidates the
benchmark suite requires more scrutiny than a large change that does not.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that modification categories for GenAI devices need clear, prespecified boundaries tied to whether a change can affect outputs and whether the existing benchmark suite remains a valid instrument for evaluating the changed device.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt a three-tier change-control structure: Tier 1 (no re-benchmarking for changes with no path to output), Tier 2 (full re-benchmarking against a locked suite at a prespecified non-inferiority margin under the QMS, with failure escalating to Tier 3), and Tier 3 (premarket submission for foundation model family/provider changes, intended use or user expansion, new modalities, agentic tool access or action scope changes, and changes the locked suite cannot validly probe).

gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: The proposal makes premarket review turn on whether a change introduces capabilities outside what the locked benchmark suite probes, i.e., whether the device's behavioral envelope has expanded beyond the validated scope.
gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The tiering distinguishes model version updates within the same foundation model family and provider (QMS-managed) from a change of foundation model family or provider (premarket submission), treating supplier identity as a determinant of evidence needs.

positions.public_summary: Proposes a three-tier change-control structure for GenAI device modifications: no re-benchmarking where changes cannot affect outputs; QMS-managed full re-benchmarking against a locked suite at a prespecified non-inferiority margin; and premarket submission for model family/provider changes, scope or modality expansion, agentic action changes, or changes the
positions.source_passage:
Applying that principle, a tiered structure might look like:
Tier 1 — no re-benchmarking.  Changes that cannot affect device outputs: user interface presentation,
logging, analytics instrumentation, infrastructure changes with no path to the output. Documented under
normal change control.
Tier 2 — full re-benchmarking against the locked suite, managed within the QMS, no premarket
submission. Model version updates within the same family and provider; prompt or template modifications
within  a  validated  structure;  retrieval  corpus  refreshes  drawing  on  a  validated  source  list;  sampling
configuration changes within a validated range. The condition is that the device passes the complete locked
benchmark  suite  at  a  prespecified  non-inferiority  margin,  with  results  documented  and  available  on
inspection. Failure at any element converts the change to Tier 3.
Tier 3 — premarket submission.  Change of foundation model family or provider; expansion of intended
use, intended user, or clinical scope; addition of a new input or output modality; any change to agentic tool
access or action scope; and any change for which the locked benchmark suite is no longer a valid instrument
— for example, a change that introduces capabilities the suite does not probe.

positions.stakeholder_concern: If a sponsor can revise both the device and the benchmark suite under a lower-tier, self-managed change pathway, non-inferiority testing against the revised instrument loses evidentiary meaning.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require that the locked benchmark suite cannot be altered under the intermediate (Tier 2) change pathway, and treat any modification of the locked suite as a Tier 3 event subject to the highest level of review.
positions.public_summary: Supports a tiered change-control approach but asks FDA to require that the locked benchmark suite itself be unmodifiable under the intermediate tier, since a sponsor revising device and evaluation instrument together renders non-inferiority findings meaningless; suite changes should trigger the highest tier.
positions.source_passage:
The essential safeguard is that the benchmark suite itself cannot be modified within Tier 2.  If the sponsor
can  revise  the  instrument  and  the  device  together,  non-inferiority  against  the  revised  instrument  is
meaningless. Modification of the locked suite should always be a Tier 3 event.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues the existing PCCP construct assumes modifications can be enumerated in advance, which fails for generative devices because the change space is genuinely open (e.g., unforeseeable third-party model versions or prompt refinements suggested by experience).
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt an 'invariant-based' PCCP that prespecifies what must remain true after any change rather than the changes themselves: an escrowed, immutable benchmark suite; acceptance thresholds including subgroup thresholds and non-inferiority margin; an independent verification protocol executed before changes reach users; rollback criteria, maximum time-to-rollback and demonstrated rollback capability; change categories defined by a tier boundary rather than enumeration; and documentation and notification obligations per change.

gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: The proposal shifts change control from enumerating modifications to locking a behavioral envelope—fixed benchmarks, thresholds, and rollback conditions that must hold after any change.
gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: It notes sponsors cannot enumerate model versions a third-party provider will release, implying invariants and verification must govern supplier-initiated changes.

positions.public_summary: Accepts adapting PCCPs to generative devices but says prespecifying changes is unworkable given an open change space. Proposes an invariant-based PCCP locking escrowed benchmarks, subgroup acceptance thresholds, independent pre-release verification, demonstrated rollback with time limits, tier-defined change categories, and notification duties.
positions.source_passage:
The current PCCP construct prespecifies what will change  — the modification, the methods to implement
and validate it, the impact assessment. For generative devices this fails, not because sponsors are unwilling
but because the change space is genuinely open: a sponsor cannot enumerate in advance the model versions a
provider will release or the prompt refinements that experience will suggest.
The adaptation is to invert what is locked. An invariant-based PCCP prespecifies not the change but what
must remain true after any change:
The evaluation instrument — the complete benchmark suite, escrowed and immutable.
The acceptance thresholds, including subgroup-level thresholds and the non-inferiority margin.
The verification protocol — what is run, in what order, by whom, with what independence, before any
change reaches users.
The  rollback  criteria  and  mechanism,  including  maximum  time-to-rollback  and  the  technical
demonstration that rollback is achievable.
The  change categories in scope , defined by the Tier 2 boundary above rather than by enumeration of
specific changes.
The documentation and notification obligations attaching to each change.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues that a benchmark-anchored change-control construct is circular and provides no assurance if a sponsor can alter the benchmark suite at the same time it modifies the device, because the measuring instrument would no longer be fixed.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require that the benchmark suite be escrowed (locked) and that any change to the benchmark suite itself be treated at the highest review tier (Tier 3), rather than being optional elements of the framework.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment warns that leaving sponsors free to revise the evaluation instrument alongside the device delegates control over the assurance baseline to the manufacturer, voiding its evidentiary value.

positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts a benchmark-anchored change-control approach only if the benchmark suite is escrowed and locked, with any change to the suite subject to the highest (Tier 3) review. Otherwise, sponsors modifying benchmarks alongside devices would render the framework circular and non-assuring.
positions.source_passage:
The construct depends entirely on the integrity of the locked instrument. If the sponsor can modify the
benchmark suite while modifying the device, the whole thing is circular and provides no assurance at all.
Escrow of the suite, and Tier 3 treatment of any change to it, are not optional features of this proposal — they
are the proposal.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Devices built on third-party models may be exposed to provider-initiated changes if the underlying model endpoint is not version-pinned; the commenter treats the inability to pin a version, or use of a provider that lacks pinning and change notification, as a design deficiency rather than an acceptable residual risk.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should explicitly state that GenAI-enabled devices relying on third-party models are expected to execute against a pinned, version-identified model endpoint as a design control expectation, and that lack of pinning or of provider change notice must be remediated.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The comment frames third-party model provider practices—offering version pinning and change notification—as a supplier qualification and design control matter rather than a manufacturer-only monitoring duty.
gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: It ties continued assurance of the deployed device to control over the specific model version actually executing in production, beyond premarket evaluation.

positions.public_summary: Endorses FDA addressing third-party model changes but asks CDRH to go further: state as a design control expectation that devices execute against a pinned, version-identified model endpoint, treating inability to pin or absent provider change notice as a design deficiency.
positions.source_passage:
Treat version pinning as a design control expectation.  CDRH should state that a GenAI-enabled device
relying on a third-party model is expected to execute against a pinned, version-identified model endpoint, and
that the inability to pin — or reliance on a provider that does not offer pinning with change notice — is a
design deficiency to be addressed, not a residual risk to be accepted. This is the single highest-leverage
statement CDRH could make in this area, and it would immediately reshape provider offerings in the medical
device segment.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Device manufacturers may not have enough advance warning of third-party foundation model changes to complete re-evaluation before the change takes effect, and pinned model versions may be retired too quickly.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require contractual advance change-notice from foundation model developers with a defined minimum notice period sufficient to complete Tier 2 re-benchmarking before a change takes effect, plus a minimum deprecation window for pinned model versions.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The comment addresses upstream supplier obligations—advance change notice and version deprecation timelines—as a precondition for the device manufacturer's ability to maintain assurance.

positions.public_summary: Supports contractual mechanisms for third-party model changes but asks FDA to require a defined minimum advance change-notice period, long enough to complete Tier 2 re-benchmarking before a change takes effect, and a minimum deprecation window for pinned model versions.
positions.source_passage:
Require contractual change notice with a defined minimum period , sufficient to complete the Tier 2 re-
benchmarking described above before a change takes effect, together with a minimum deprecation window
for pinned versions.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Contractual assurances from third-party model hosts cannot be verified in real time, so silent upstream changes to a hosted model could go undetected during deployment.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should describe continuous 'canary' monitoring — a small fixed probe suite of inputs with known expected outputs run frequently against the live endpoint — as an expected element of postmarket monitoring for any device built on a third-party hosted model.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The comment argues that contractual or supplier-based assurances about a third-party hosted model cannot be verified in real time and must be replaced by direct technical verification of endpoint stability.
gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: It proposes an ongoing, high-frequency automated probe running against the live deployed endpoint as a low-cost mechanism for continuous assurance rather than point-in-time evaluation.

positions.public_summary: Supports postmarket monitoring for devices using third-party hosted models, but asks FDA to go further: describe continuous "canary" probe testing — fixed inputs with known expected outputs run frequently against the live endpoint — as an expected element, since contracts cannot be verified in real
positions.source_passage:
Require continuous canary monitoring, because contracts cannot be verified in real time.  A small, fixed
probe suite — a set of inputs with known expected outputs — executed against the live endpoint at high
frequency  provides  direct  detection  of  silent  upstream  change.  This  is  inexpensive,  technically
straightforward, and the only mechanism I am aware of that verifies rather than assumes endpoint stability. I
recommend CDRH describe it as an expected element of postmarket monitoring for any device on a third-
party hosted model.

positions.stakeholder_concern: When a foundation model provider deprecates a pinned version, the manufacturer is compelled to migrate, and the device then runs on a materially different model regardless of whether the change was voluntary; treating such involuntary migrations as lower-risk changes would understate that reality.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should classify provider-forced model migrations in the highest change tier (Tier 3) and explicitly foreclose lighter treatment based on involuntariness, and expect manufacturers to address deprecation contingencies in design planning, including maintaining a validated fallback.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The comment centers on third-party model providers' version deprecation decisions forcing changes to the device, requiring manufacturers to manage supplier lifecycle risk in advance.
gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: It asks that continuity of validated device behavior be assured through pre-planned fallback versions rather than emergency response when an upstream model is withdrawn.

positions.public_summary: Commenter agrees with tiered change control but urges FDA to treat provider-forced migration off a deprecated pinned model as a highest-tier change, rejecting lighter treatment because migration was involuntary, and to expect pre-planned contingencies including a validated fallback version.
positions.source_passage:
Treat provider-forced migration as a Tier 3 change. When a provider deprecates a pinned version and the
manufacturer must migrate, the resulting device is running on a different model. That it was involuntary does
not change what it is, and the paper should foreclose the argument that forced migrations warrant lighter
treatment.  Manufacturers  should  be  expected  to  plan  for  this  contingency  —  including  maintaining  a
validated fallback — as part of design planning rather than handling it as an emergency.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Manufacturers and CDRH currently must infer dependency risk on third-party foundation models rather than assess it from documented facts about model versioning, deprecation, and change notification.
positions.requested_fda_action: Establish/maintain the Foundation Model Master File as a standing, current record that documents model versioning, deprecation timelines, and change-notification practices so dependency risk can be assessed directly during review.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The comment frames upstream model suppliers' versioning, deprecation, and change-notification practices as information that must be documented and assessable, treating supplier practices as a quality input to device assurance.

positions.public_summary: Comment sees the greatest value of a Foundation Model Master File in providing a standing, current record of a model's versioning, deprecation, and change-notification practices, enabling CDRH and manufacturers to assess dependency risk directly rather than by inference.
positions.source_passage:
I would also note that this is where a Foundation Model MAF (Question 25) would deliver the most value: a
standing, current record of a model's versioning, deprecation, and change-notification practices would let
CDRH and manufacturers assess dependency risk directly rather than by inference.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter agrees that foundation model developers have little intrinsic incentive to disclose safety-relevant limitations, since medical devices are a small share of their revenue and disclosure carries competitive and litigation exposure, so a purely voluntary MAF program is unlikely to attract broad participation.
positions.requested_fda_action: Establish the voluntary Foundation Model MAF program but pair it with a manufacturer-side default: absent an MAF, the device manufacturer must independently and at its own cost characterize the underlying model (training data provenance to the extent determinable, contamination assessment, known failure modes, version and deprecation practices, subgroup performance) or the submission is incomplete.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The comment addresses how to obtain quality and safety information about upstream foundation model suppliers who are outside FDA's direct reach, proposing procurement pressure as the enforcement mechanism.
gap_explanations.evidence_burden_commercial_viability: It explicitly relies on the cost and technical infeasibility of independent model characterization to shift manufacturer procurement behavior, making evidence burden the operative lever.

positions.public_summary: Agrees the voluntary MAF program faces a real incentive problem but recommends creating it anyway, paired with a default rule placing the full model-characterization burden (provenance, contamination, failure modes, versioning, subgroup performance) on manufacturers when no MAF exists, creating commercial pressure for developer participation.
positions.source_passage:
The paper's candor about the incentive problem is warranted. Foundation model developers serve markets in
which  medical  devices  are  a  small  fraction  of  revenue;  disclosure  of  safety-relevant  limitations  carries
competitive and litigation exposure; and a voluntary program asking them to document weaknesses for a
regulator overseeing someone else's product is unlikely to attract broad participation on its own merits.
I nonetheless recommend CDRH create it, because the mechanism that makes it work is not the model
developer's incentive — it is the device manufacturer's.
Pair  the  voluntary  MAF  with  a  manufacturer-side  default:  where  an  MAF  is  absent,  the  device
manufacturer bears the full characterization burden for the underlying model. Training data provenance
to  the  extent  determinable,  contamination  assessment,  known  failure  modes,  version  and  deprecation
practices, subgroup performance characterization — all of it, generated independently at the manufacturer's
cost, or the submission is incomplete.
That default creates a procurement preference. Device manufacturers will strongly prefer model providers
that maintain a current MAF, because the alternative is expensive and often technically impossible. Providers
will then face a commercial reason to participate that has nothing to do with regulatory goodwill.

positions.stakeholder_concern: A Foundation Model MAF is only useful if it contains specific, safety-relevant items (version lineage, training data cutoff, change/deprecation policy, known failure modes, safety and refusal behavior, developer evaluations, medical fine-tuning) and is kept current; a static snapshot would not support contamination analysis or timely detection of third-party model changes.
positions.requested_fda_action: Specify a defined MAF content set covering model identity/version lineage, training data cutoff, versioning, change notification and deprecation policy, known limitations and failure modes, safety/refusal behavior, developer evaluation results, and medical-domain training. Impose a currency requirement obligating MAF updates within a defined period after any model change.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The comment defines the specific upstream disclosures (version lineage, data cutoff, failure modes, deprecation policy) a device manufacturer needs from a foundation model supplier to sustain assurance.
gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: The proposed currency requirement addresses maintaining valid safety information over time as upstream models change, rather than at a single premarket point.

positions.public_summary: Endorses Foundation Model Master Files, but specifies required content: model identity and version lineage, training data cutoff, versioning/change-notification and deprecation policy, known failure modes, safety and refusal behavior, developer evaluations, and medical fine-tuning; urges requiring updates within a defined period after any model change.
positions.source_passage:
Suggested MAF content: model identity and version lineage; training data cutoff date (essential for the
contamination analysis under Question 10); versioning, change notification, and deprecation policy (essential
for Question 24); known limitations and documented failure modes; safety training and refusal behavior;
evaluation results the developer has generated; and any medical-domain-specific training or fine-tuning. A
currency requirement — the MAF must be updated within a defined period of any model change — is what
makes it useful rather than a snapshot.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that a Foundation Model Master File could be misread as evidence establishing the safety or effectiveness of devices built on that model, displacing evaluation of the device itself.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should explicitly frame the MAF as contextual information supporting, not substituting for, evaluation of the final user-facing device as configured for deployment, consistent with the paper's stated unit of evaluation.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The comment addresses how information supplied by upstream foundation model developers should and should not be relied upon in assuring the downstream device.

positions.public_summary: Endorses the paper's position that the final deployed device is the unit of evaluation, and cautions that a Foundation Model Master File should be framed only as context for device evaluation, never as evidence of a device's safety or effectiveness.
positions.source_passage:
I would add one caution: an MAF should never be treated as establishing the safety or effectiveness of any
device built on the model. The paper's statement that the unit of evaluation is the final user-facing device as
configured for deployment is correct and important, and the MAF should be framed as context for that
evaluation, not as a partial substitute for it.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Per-step accuracy metrics overstate end-to-end reliability for multi-step agentic devices, since 95% per-step accuracy yields roughly 60% success across a ten-step task, and error compounding worsens as sequences lengthen.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should explicitly state that acceptance criteria for agentic GenAI-enabled devices be set at the level of the completed task, with evaluation measuring task completion rather than step accuracy.
positions.public_summary: Commenter endorses attention to agentic devices but urges FDA to state explicitly that acceptance criteria and evaluation address completed-task performance rather than per-step accuracy, citing compounding error across multi-step sequences and the ease of generating step-level metrics.
positions.source_passage:
Trajectory-level  acceptance  criteria. Per-step  performance  is  a  misleading  summary  of  end-to-end
reliability. A device that completes each step correctly 95% of the time completes a ten-step task correctly
about 60% of the time, and that arithmetic is unforgiving as sequences lengthen. Acceptance criteria must be
stated at the level of the completed task, and evaluation must measure task completion rather than step
accuracy. I recommend CDRH state this explicitly, because step-level metrics are far easier to generate and
will otherwise be offered.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that an agentic device's scope of actions can expand incrementally—adding tools, write operations, or affected external systems—moving a deployment from low to high risk without any regulatory event marking the transition.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require sponsors to submit an enumerated inventory of every action the system can take, each classified by reversibility and consequence of erroneous execution; require explicit qualified-user confirmation for irreversible actions; and treat the inventory as a locked specification whose expansion constitutes a Tier 3 change under the Question 22 change framework.

gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: The comment identifies uncontrolled expansion of an agent's action scope as a silent migration from low-risk to high-risk operation unaccompanied by any regulatory checkpoint.
gap_explanations.delegated_authority: It proposes bounding the authority delegated to the agent by enumerating permitted actions and requiring explicit qualified-user confirmation before irreversible ones.

positions.public_summary: Supports the agentic and change-control framework but asks FDA to require an enumerated inventory of all system actions classified by reversibility and consequence of error, explicit qualified-user confirmation for irreversible actions, and treatment of scope expansion as a Tier 3 change.
positions.source_passage:
Action inventory with irreversibility classification. I recommend sponsors submit an enumerated inventory
of every action the system can take — every tool, every write operation, every external system it can affect
— each classified by reversibility and by the consequence of erroneous execution. Irreversible actions should
require explicit confirmation by a qualified user, and the inventory should be treated as a locked specification
whose expansion is a Tier 3 change under the framework in Question 22. Uncontrolled expansion of an
agent's action scope is the most likely path from a low-risk deployment to a high-risk one without any
regulatory event marking the transition.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Agentic GenAI devices could hold broader tool permissions than their intended use requires; the commenter views least-privilege, per-deployment scoping as standard security practice already reflected in CDRH cybersecurity expectations.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expect agentic systems to hold the narrowest permissions sufficient for the intended use, scoped per deployment, and cross-reference CDRH's existing cybersecurity expectations rather than creating a parallel treatment in the paper.

gap_explanations.cybersecurity_as_safety: The comment treats security permission controls as integral to safe agentic device operation and urges alignment with existing cybersecurity expectations rather than a separate framework.
gap_explanations.delegated_authority: It frames the core control as limiting the scope of tool access and permissions granted to an autonomous agent to the minimum needed for the intended use.

positions.public_summary: Supports addressing agentic autonomy but asks FDA to specify least-privilege tool permissions scoped to each deployment and intended use, and to cross-reference CDRH's existing cybersecurity expectations instead of developing a separate, parallel treatment in the discussion paper.
positions.source_passage:
Least-privilege  tool  access. Agentic  systems  should  hold  the  narrowest  permissions  sufficient  for  the
intended use, scoped per deployment. This is standard security practice and maps directly onto CDRH's
existing cybersecurity expectations; I recommend the paper cross-reference them rather than developing a
parallel treatment.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Without audit logs capturing the full agentic trajectory — inputs, intermediate reasoning artifacts, tool calls, returned values, actions taken, and the model version and configuration in effect — root cause analysis of harmful outcomes is impossible and corrective action becomes guesswork. The commenter states this also prevents discharging the complaint-handling obligations discussed under Question 21.
positions.requested_fda_action: Make the adequacy of audit logging an explicit premarket review element for agentic GenAI-enabled devices, rather than treating it as an assumed postmarket capability.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment focuses on autonomous multi-step action and tool use, arguing that actions taken by the agent must be reconstructable after the fact for accountability and corrective action.
gap_explanations.operational_harm: The concern is the investigability of harmful outcomes arising from an agent's full execution trajectory, not just the correctness of a single output.

positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts the framework's attention to agentic oversight but asks FDA to require audit logging that reconstructs full agentic trajectories — inputs, tool calls, actions, model version and configuration — as an explicit premarket review element, arguing root cause analysis and complaint handling otherwise fail.
positions.source_passage:
Audit logging sufficient for post-hoc reconstruction. When an agentic system produces a harmful outcome,
the investigation must be able to reconstruct the full trajectory — inputs, intermediate reasoning artifacts
where available, tool calls, returned values, actions taken, and the model version and configuration in effect.
Without this, root cause analysis is not possible, corrective action is guesswork, and the complaint-handling
obligations under Question 21 cannot be discharged. I recommend audit logging adequacy be an explicit
premarket review element for agentic devices rather than a postmarket assumption.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues that compounding errors in agentic devices make end-to-end performance hardest to establish premarket while errors propagate fastest and are least reversible after deployment, so accepting greater premarket uncertainty is particularly ill-suited to this device category.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should treat agentic GenAI-enabled devices as presumptively ineligible for the reduced-premarket-evidence pathway that relies on greater postmarket monitoring.

gap_explanations.operational_harm: The comment emphasizes that agentic errors propagate rapidly and are least reversible once deployed, a harm dynamic not captured by the premarket-uncertainty trade as framed.
gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The concern arises from autonomous multi-step action chains where compounding errors occur without intervening human review.

positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts the postmarket-reliance concept generally but argues it fits agentic devices poorly, since their end-to-end performance is hardest to establish premarket and errors compound fastest and are least reversible. Recommends CDRH presumptively exclude agentic devices from any reduced-premarket-evidence pathway.
positions.source_passage:
I would also note that the compounding-error arithmetic above interacts badly with the premarket-uncertainty
trade proposed in Question 18. Agentic devices are where end-to-end performance is hardest to establish
premarket,  and  simultaneously  where  errors  propagate  fastest  and  are  least  reversible  postmarket.  I
recommend CDRH treat agentic devices as presumptively outside the reduced-premarket-evidence pathway.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that without an explicit, published mapping from risk tier to required evidence, the competency-based framework will lack predictability and will not in practice be least burdensome.
positions.requested_fda_action: Publish the mapping between risk tiers and the corresponding level of premarket evidence expected, so sponsors can anticipate evidence requirements.

gap_explanations.evidence_burden_commercial_viability: The comment ties predictability of the risk-to-evidence mapping directly to whether the framework actually reduces evidentiary burden on sponsors.

positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts a risk-based, competency-based evidence framework but asks FDA to publish an explicit risk-tier-to-evidence mapping, arguing that without such predictability the approach will not in practice be least burdensome.
positions.source_passage:
Publish  the  risk-tier-to-evidence  mapping. Predictability  is  the  mechanism  by  which  risk-based
frameworks reduce burden. Without it, "competency-based" and "least burdensome" will not describe the
same thing.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that the proposed competency-based framework could create artifacts parallel to the risk management, design control, and change control documentation manufacturers already maintain under ISO 14971 and the QMSR.
positions.requested_fda_action: Build the framework on existing quality system and risk management infrastructure rather than requiring separate parallel artifacts, and explain in the paper how the new elements relate to established QMSR and ISO 14971 processes.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts the framework's direction but asks FDA to ground it in existing ISO 14971 risk files, design controls, and QMSR change control procedures instead of creating parallel artifacts, and to clarify in the paper how these elements relate.
positions.source_passage:
Integrate with existing quality system and risk management infrastructure.  Manufacturers maintain
ISO 14971 risk files, design controls, and change control procedures under the QMSR. The framework
should draw on these rather than establishing parallel artifacts, and the paper should state how the pieces
relate.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter notes that the paper defers the question of statutory authority, yet several proposals — enforceable postmarket conditions with automatic consequences, third-party recognition regimes, and obligations reaching foundation model developers who are not device manufacturers — may sit at or beyond the limits of CDRH's existing authorities.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should return to and identify explicitly which elements of the framework it can implement under current authority and which would require new legislation from Congress, so stakeholders know which parts to build toward.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment questions the legal basis for third-party recognition regimes and postmarket conditions carrying automatic consequences.
gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: It flags that obligations extending to foundation model developers who are not device manufacturers may exceed existing authorities.

positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts the framework's direction but urges CDRH to stop deferring the legal-authority question, arguing that enforceable postmarket conditions with automatic consequences, third-party recognition regimes, and obligations on non-manufacturer foundation model developers may require congressional action; stakeholders need that clarity.
positions.source_passage:
Identify  which  elements  require  new  legal  authority. The  paper  expressly  defers  this  question.  I
understand why, but I would encourage CDRH to return to it, because several proposals — enforceable
postmarket conditions with automatic consequences, third-party recognition regimes, obligations touching
foundation model developers who are not device manufacturers — appear to sit at or beyond the edge of
existing authorities. Stakeholders assessing which parts of this framework to build toward would benefit
from knowing which parts CDRH can implement and which would require Congress.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter observes that the discussion paper's competency-based framing is oriented toward enabling market entry and worries it may be read as an authorization pathway rather than a genuine evaluation framework capable of a negative conclusion.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should explicitly state that the competency-based framework contemplates the outcome that a given intended use is not currently supportable by available evidence.
positions.public_summary: Accepts the competency-based framework in principle but asks CDRH to state explicitly that it can conclude an intended use is not currently supportable by available evidence, so it is understood as an evaluation framework rather than an authorization pathway.
positions.source_passage:
Preserve  the  option  to  say  no. The  paper's  framing  is  oriented  toward  enabling  market  entry,
appropriately  so  given  its  purpose.  But  a  competency-based  framework  should  also  be  capable  of
concluding  that  a  given  intended  use  is  not  currently  supportable  by  available  evidence.  I  would
encourage CDRH to state that the framework contemplates that outcome, so that it is understood as an
evaluation framework rather than an authorization pathway.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter's central concern is that the framework's regulatory flexibility outpaces the supporting infrastructure: benchmarks that cannot yet be trusted, unsettled postmarket reportability rules, third-party foundation model dependencies manufacturers cannot currently control, and non-existent third-party assessment capacity.
positions.requested_fda_action: Sequence the approach so that the enabling infrastructure — trustworthy benchmarks, clear postmarket reportability rules, mechanisms for third-party model dependency control, and qualified third-party assessment capacity — is established before the flexible evidentiary pathways are relied upon.

gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: The commenter states that qualified third-party assessment capacity to support the framework does not yet exist, limiting whether the approach can be executed at scale.
gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The comment identifies third-party foundation model dependencies that manufacturers cannot presently control as a structural precondition the framework assumes but does not supply.

positions.public_summary: The commenter accepts the framework's direction but argues its flexibility currently outruns necessary infrastructure — untrustworthy benchmarks, unsettled postmarket reportability rules, uncontrollable third-party model dependencies, and absent third-party assessment capacity — and asks FDA to build that infrastructure before relying on flexible pathways.
positions.source_passage:
My central concern is that the framework's flexibility currently outruns the infrastructure needed to make
flexibility safe: benchmarks that cannot yet be trusted, postmarket monitoring whose reportability rules are
unsettled,  third-party  model  dependencies  that  manufacturers  cannot  presently  control,  and  third-party
assessment capacity that does not yet exist. Each of these is addressable, and several are addressable now. But
the flexibility and the infrastructure should arrive in that order — infrastructure first — rather than the
reverse.
